title: Karma Cannot Bind
author: Zhanran
excerpt: At the moment of death, karma cannot bind, and wherever one turns one is free.

inline.s: With a sincere heart and right intention cultivate the root,
let not following an arising thought be the standard.
Take the self-nature as one's essence; do not identify with the physical body;
take the numinous knowing as one's own mind; do not identify with delusive thoughts.
When delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them,
then at the moment of death karma cannot bind, and wherever one turns one is free.
"All living beings are endowed with the nature of awakening—luminous, still, and void—in no way different from the Buddhas. Only because

from beginningless kalpas they have never awakened, deludedly clinging to the body as the mark of self, they give rise to feelings of love and aversion. Following emotion they create karma; following karma they receive its retribution—birth, aging, sickness, and death, revolving through long kalpas. Yet the nature of awakening within the body has never known birth or death: as in a dream one is driven about, while the body itself remains at ease; as water turns to ice, yet its wetness does not change. If one can awaken to this nature

as the Dharma body, which of itself was never born—what need is there of anything to rely upon? Luminous and never dimmed, clearly ever knowing, it has come from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet the deluded clinging of many lives has become a habitual nature; joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure flow on in subtle streams. Though the true principle is suddenly reached, these feelings are hard to erase all at once; one must constantly be aware and aware again, diminishing them ever further. As the wind suddenly stops and the waves gradually subside—how could the cultivation of a single lifetime equal the power and function of the Buddhas? Only take emptiness and stillness as one's own essence, not identifying with the physical body; take the numinous knowing as one's own mind, not identifying with delusive thoughts.
When delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them
—then at the moment of death, karma of itself cannot bind.

Though there be an intermediate state, wherever one turns one is free; among gods or among humans, one may dwell at will. If the thoughts of love and aversion are already extinguished, one no longer receives the body of separate existence
(no more of the birth-and-death of separate existence)

—then of itself one exchanges the short for the long, the coarse for the subtle. If the subtle streams are all stilled, and the great wisdom of perfect awakening alone stands luminous, then responding to conditions one manifests hundreds of billions of bodies to deliver living beings of karmic affinity—this is called being a Buddha."
(Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[Taking emptiness and stillness as one's own essence]This is said from the ultimate standpoint. Because the practice of Chan in the present life is precisely about ending the birth-and-death of separate existence, taking the self-nature as one's essence makes it relatively easy to comprehend and grasp. [Numinous knowing]This is the knowing of emptiness and stillness. [Intermediate state]The intermediate body, also called the "between," is a body of subtle matter formed by transformation that sustains life after death and before one takes rebirth; this transformation body is the intermediate body. During the first forty-nine days it dies and is reborn once every seven days, passing through seven such births and deaths, awaiting the arrangement of karmic conditions before it takes rebirth.
Here three stages of practice are explained:

1. Subduing afflictions. Its requirement is: when delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them. (Please pay special attention to the word "none.") Its effect is: at the moment of death, karma cannot bind; though there be an intermediate state, wherever one turns one is free; among gods or among humans, one may dwell at will.

2. Cutting off afflictions. Its requirement is: the thoughts of love and aversion are already extinguished. Its effect is: ending birth and death (no more of the birth-and-death of separate existence) and departing the three realms.

3. Realizing Buddhahood. Its requirement is: the subtle streams are all stilled, and the great wisdom of perfect awakening alone stands luminous. Its effect is: no more of the birth-and-death of transformation; responding to conditions one manifests hundreds of billions of bodies to deliver living beings of karmic affinity—this is called being a Buddha.

[Birth-and-death of separate existence]Living beings in the three realms and six paths, owing to the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma, have limited lifetimes and distinct bodies, so their birth and death is called "birth-and-death of separate existence." One who ends this birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth and departs the three realms. [Birth-and-death of transformation]The sages of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thought, have ended the birth-and-death of separate existence. In the course of cultivation, deluded thinking gradually dies away and realization gradually grows; this passage from delusion to awakening differs in each period. The move from one period into the next is exactly like a death and rebirth, and so it is called "birth-and-death of transformation." One who ends this birth-and-death fully realizes Buddhahood.

All dharmas are like a dream; all sages say the same. Thus delusive thoughts are originally still, and sense objects are originally empty. The empty and still mind is luminous in knowing and never dimmed.
This very knowing of emptiness and stillness is your true nature.

Whether deluded or awakened, the mind is of itself knowing; it is not born from conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The single word "knowing" is the gate of all mysteries. Because of the delusion beginningless in time, one deludedly clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and anger. If a good spiritual friend points it out, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of emptiness and stillness. And since this knowing is without thought and without form, who is there to be the mark of self or the mark of a person?
Perceiving that all marks are empty, the mind is of itself without thought
When a thought arises, one is immediately aware of it; being aware of it, it is immediately gone. The wondrous gateway of practice lies only here.

Therefore, though one may cultivate all practices, the only essential is the absence of thought. Once one gains the view of no-thought, then love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally brighten, evil karma is naturally cut off, and meritorious practice naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are not marks, one naturally practices without practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are cut off. When arising and ceasing are extinguished, still illumination appears, and its function is inexhaustible—this is called being a Buddha.
Preface to the Collected Notes on the Source of Chan

[Perceiving that all marks are empty, the mind is of itself without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware of it; being aware of it, it is immediately gone. The wondrous gateway of practice lies only here]Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. When a delusive thought arises, one must immediately realize that this is taking illusion as real and being turned by illusory marks. Once one realizes this, the delusive thought instantly vanishes. The wondrous gateway of practice is right here!
As to whether one can be in control oneself at the hour of death, Master Guifeng's verse says
(see the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
Delusion follows the thoughts of emotion; at death one is dragged by karma;
Awakening is not governed by emotion; at death one can transform karma.
Now the two verses are explained as follows:

The first verse speaks of the karma that one creates. At the moment a thought arises, whether one follows emotion or relies on wisdom (the wisdom that understands principle) is the dividing line between delusion and awakening.
Doing meaningful deeds—this is the awakened mind.
and only then act—this is the awakened mind,
Doing meaningless deeds—this is a deluded, scattered mind.
This is a sheer waste of energy and time,
and it even creates evil karma.
is like the drunkard or madman of the world:
where he goes he does not choose the place,
what he does he does not weigh right and wrong,
he does not select meaning or benefit
doing whatever he wants—this is the
One who acts following emotion is bound by karma at death and is reborn according to his karma; one who acts relying on wisdom is free at death and is not bound by karma.
Delusion follows the thoughts of emotion,
at death one is dragged by karma
The deluded, scattered mind turns along with emotional thoughts (acting with the stream of karma), so at death one is dragged by karma.
not using the wisdom that understands principle
to choose between right and wrong,
so at death one is dragged
Awakening is not governed by emotion,
at death one can transform karma
The awakened mind does not turn along with emotional thoughts (acting against the stream of karma), so at death one can transform karma (karma cannot bind).

When emotion wants to act, but on examining principle one sees that it should not be done, one must stop at once. When emotion does not want to act, but in accord with principle one sees that it should be done, one must go and do it at once. Only by following the principle of right and wrong, and not the feelings of love and aversion, can one be free from karma's binding at the moment of death; though there be an intermediate state, wherever one turns one is free, dwelling at will among gods or among humans.

In short, if what one does from morning to night is governed by emotional thoughts, then at death one is dragged by karma and reborn according to it: wholesome karma leads to the wholesome realms, evil karma leads to the evil realms. If one's deeds rely on the wisdom of awakening and not on emotional thoughts, then at death one is in control of oneself and free wherever one turns. To judge whether one's destination at death is autonomous or not, one need only examine how one usually employs the mind—whether it is free or bound in the presence of sense objects.

Therefore, in ordinary times one must train in the practice of "aware illumination that turns a thought." One must be constantly on the alert, training this mind so that it can rein in at the brink of the cliff: stop as soon as one says stop, let go as soon as one says let go. One must be quick to recognize and quick to turn, so that burning affliction suddenly becomes a ground of cool clarity. On this, Master Hanshan, in the "Reply to Yang Yuanru, the Marshal" of his Collection of the Roaming of Dreams, gives a penetrating instruction, now annotated as follows:

[The ancients said, "In the field of heat and turmoil, a cool eye is hard to bear." Because the three realms offer no peace, like a burning house, none who enter and leave them escape being scorched and boiled. If one seeks a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, only one with a cool eye can gain it. If one can, in a single instant, make the thought cool, then at once one sees the great earth all as ice, and by nature no longer makes a home in the world of body and mind. These persons of great power from of old, who sport in the field of birth and death, who turn the dust of toil into Buddhist deeds and transform affliction into bodhi, rely merely on a single cool eye and a single cool heart; what further spiritual powers or wondrous functions do they have?]

The ancients said, "Though in the field of heat and turmoil everything stirs the mind, it cannot withstand being regarded with a cool eye." Because the three realms offer no peace, like a burning house, none who enter and leave them escape being scorched and boiled. If one seeks a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, only one with a cool eye can manage it. If one views the world with a cool eye until the thought of the present moment becomes cool, then at once one sees the great earth all as ice, and by nature will not make a home in the world of body and mind. These persons of great power from of old, who sport in the field of birth and death, who turn the dust of toil into Buddhist deeds and transform affliction into bodhi—they rely merely on a single cool eye and a single cool heart! What further spiritual powers or wondrous functions are there?

[The three realms offer no peace, like a burning house]The Lotus Sutra says: "The three realms offer no peace, like a burning house, filled with all suffering, dreadful to behold; always there is the distress of birth, aging, sickness, and death; such fires blaze without ceasing." [Merely relying on a single cool eye and a single cool heart]This means: when the mind is empty, objects are empty of themselves; the myriad dharmas are unbound, originally free. The Diamond Sutra says: "All marks are false." "Do not grasp at marks, abiding in thusness without moving." In these two passages, "All marks are false" is the cool eye; "Do not grasp at marks, abiding in thusness without moving" is the cool heart. In this sentence, "qu" means "he."

[This saying is very easy to know but very hard to see. Consider that the Buddhas and the patriarchs used this single phrase, "all dharmas are like a dream," as the essential road to transcending the world. Yet the wise and the foolish of the world can alike all say "life is like a dream." The words seem the same, but the meaning is not. In truth they have never truly, with a single eye, seen through life as a dream. If one has truly seen through it, then naturally one can, at every turn of honor and disgrace, benefit and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, fling one's arm and go; who would dare to oppose his edge?]

This saying ("In the field of heat and turmoil, a cool eye is hard to bear") is very easy to know, but its true meaning is very hard to see. Just as the Buddhas and the patriarchs used this single phrase, "all dharmas are like a dream," as the essential road to transcending the world—yet how few see its true meaning? And the wise and the foolish of the world will alike all say, "life is like a dream." Though the words are one and the same "life is like a dream," the meaning in the words of the wise and in those of the foolish is wholly different. Though the fool says it with his mouth, in truth he has never truly, with a single eye, seen through life as a dream. If one has truly seen through it, then naturally one can, at every turn of honor and disgrace, benefit and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, turn and go; who could stop him? (The carp has slipped free of the golden hook, wagging its head and tail, it comes no more.)
[Flinging the arm]To swing the arm and walk away—leaving without a backward glance.

[In truth, within it there is nothing very mysterious. As for the very first step, there is indeed a method. In dealing with the world, one must first take up the affair of the dream, set it before one's eyes, and examine it closely. One must surely—truly—watch until one reaches the point of bursting into great laughter. At this point, one suddenly feels that the usual phrase "like a dream" is wholly different. Then, at the point of that laughter, in a single thought turn the present state and place it within the dream, examining it closely. When one sees the states of deep drowsiness and reversal, suddenly one is sharply awake. Thus, looking back over one's life, all the various states one has passed through, if one seeks them truly, are utterly unobtainable. This point of utter unobtainability is the first pass by which the Buddhas and the patriarchs escape birth and death.]

In truth, within it there is nothing very mysterious. As for taking the very first step, it is not without a definite method. The method is: in dealing with the world, one must first take up this affair of the dream, set it before one's eyes, and examine it closely. One must surely and truly watch, until one sees the point of bursting into great laughter. At this point, one suddenly feels that the usual saying "life is like a dream" has a wholly different flavor. Then, at the point of that great laughter, in a single thought turn toward the present state, place it within the frame of "life is like a dream," and examine it closely. When one sees the states of deep drowsiness and reversal, suddenly one is sharply and forcefully awake. Thus, looking back over one's life, all the various states one has experienced, even if one tries to take them as real, are utterly unobtainable (completely impossible). This point of utter unobtainability is the first pass by which the Buddhas and the patriarchs escape birth and death.

[Reaching the point of bursting into great laughter]Master Hanshan's "Song of Awakening the World" says: "In life, in vain one exhausts countless schemes; after death, one leaves behind only a pair of empty hands. Joy and sorrow, parting and reunion, stir us every morn; long life and early death, poverty and wealth, occupy us all the day. Cease your striving to be strong and to win; a hundred years are wholly a stage of play. In a moment the drums and gongs fall silent, and one no longer knows where home is."
Question: Who is deluded and scattered? Who is dragged by karma at death? Who is awakened? Who is free from karma's binding at death?

Answer: The self-nature is deluded and scattered. What is dragged by karma at death is the self-nature; it is the self-nature that is reborn according to karma. The self-nature is awakened. What is free from karma's binding at death is the self-nature; it is the self-nature that is free wherever it turns.

Question: Master Guifeng spoke of three stages: subduing afflictions, cutting off afflictions, and fully realizing Buddhahood. Why does this chapter take as its title only "karma cannot bind," the fruit of subduing afflictions?

Answer: To cut off afflictions in this very life, and even to fully realize Buddhahood, is extremely good. But those who can do so are as rare as phoenix feathers; all of them laid their foundations in former lives.

Yet to accomplish "at the moment of death karma cannot bind, and wherever one turns one is free" requires no prior foundation. As long as one practices correctly and with diligent, assiduous effort in this life, anyone may in this life reach "when delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them," and so attain "at the moment of death karma cannot bind, and wherever one turns one is free."

In this way, not only does one avoid "suffering the pain of the evil realms, bobbing up and down in the vast sea of karma, not knowing in which life one might again cultivate the Dharma," but one may also freely be reborn in the Pure Lands of the Buddhas; moreover, having subdued afflictions in this life, one lays a good foundation for continuing to cultivate in the life to come, without suffering the retribution of three lives. With a single act gaining threefold benefit,
"karma cannot bind" should be the goal for which the broad community of Chan practitioners strives in this life
, and so this chapter takes it as its title.

[The retribution of three lives]Because one cultivates in this life and enjoys good fortune in the next, one relies on that fortune to do evil, leading to a fall in the life after that. Even when the karma of hell is exhausted, one is again reborn as a hungry ghost or an animal; to regain a human body is extremely difficult! So the World-Honored One, holding a little earth on his hand, asked Ānanda: "Is the earth in my hand more, or the earth of the great earth?" Ānanda replied: "The earth of the great earth is more." The Buddha said: "Those who gain a human body are like the earth in my hand; those who lose a human body are like the earth of the great earth." Hence, "through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one to rely upon"!
Question: When temptation assails one, what is to be done?

Answer: There is a saying: "If temptation attacks you with cruel force, overcome it with rational analysis and an unyielding will; every desire can be controlled."—A cool eye and a cool heart: see through it and let it go. So when temptation assails one, one immediately rouses wisdom and contemplates: when the crooked comes, deliver it with the upright; when delusion comes, deliver it with awakening; when folly comes, deliver it with wisdom; when evil comes, deliver it with good—overcoming temptation with thoroughgoing principle and a firm resolve. This practice must be done often, with constant reflection and summing up, going deeper and deeper, until within one does not turn along with thoughts and without one is not dragged along by objects.
"when delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them; then at the moment of death, karma of itself cannot bind"

"This concerns the hour of death: what is it like to die? To gain freedom over rebirth at death, one must in ordinary times do the work of "when delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them." If our delusive thoughts are not completely eradicated, and in a single instant a thought arises again, one must immediately be aware of it and not run after it. If the delusive thought is strong and, though aware, one cannot cut it off, then quickly recite the Buddha's name or a mantra, or lift up the huatou, asking whence this delusive thought comes, and so dissolve it. If one has run far off after the delusive thought before realizing it, it is already too late. The speed of awareness and the quickness of removal are a question of the strength of one's effort—just as the brightness of a candle flame differs from that of electric light. At first it illuminates, but later it can no longer see clearly; one knows only after the delusive thought has arisen long ago—this is the candlelight. When one's effort is mature, one sees a thought the instant it arises, like a strong light shining before one, so that every pit and pothole is clearly seen, and walking a night road one does not fall into holes or ditches—this is the electric light. This reaches the stage of stillness that is ever illumining, and illumination that is ever still: one no longer makes an effort to illumine, but illumines naturally. Within this there is a great difference of depth in one's effort. One must be mindful at all times, applying effort closely. If in twenty-four hours one applies effort for only an hour or two and is idle for the other twenty-two, that is far too lax, and one's effort will hardly advance. Therefore, within the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying, one must apply effort at all times and be mindful at all times, so that one's effort advances. Moreover, when a delusive thought arises, one must not run after "any" of them. It is not that one judges some delusive thought good and runs after it. Someone dreams a good dream and, on waking, cannot bear to let it go, still thinking of it. The dream is originally false—why cling to it? If in a dream you were emperor, are you truly emperor? If in a dream you gained a great ingot of gold, did you truly gain it? To cling to it—is that not folly! People are just this foolish! Master Guifeng, with kind and patient words, tells us, "when delusive thoughts arise, follow none of them," do not run after them. If we truly accomplish this, then "at the moment of death, karma cannot bind." To bind means to tie up. All living beings run after karma! Those with wholesome karma ascend to heaven; those with evil karma fall into hell. If one truly can, when a delusive thought arises, not run after it, then karma cannot tie you up, and you are free."
A Detailed Explanation of the Direct Discourse on the True Mind
The Essentials of the Mind of Baiyun (Precious Book of Mind-Contemplation)
